pa01.text: Start with Sivakasi, in far-south Tamil Nadu. It sits in the rain shadow of the western hills. Little rain. Dry soil. Hard farming.

pa02.text: And a hundred years ago, it made no fireworks. It didn't even make matches.

pa03.text: Yet today, by the industry's own count, between eighty and ninety percent of India's fireworks come from here.

pa04.text: A dry town. A craft with no past. And almost every firework in India. All three are true. So how?

pa05.text: Four pieces answer it. A matchbox. A pair of hands. The sun. And, last, a printing press and a war. One at a time.

pb01.text: Find India on the globe. Now slide down to its far south, to Tamil Nadu.

pb02.text: Three things to keep in mind. A match. A Bengal light, which is a match that burns in colour. And a firework.

pc01.text: Go back to nineteen twenty-two. Matches are made in Calcutta, today's Kolkata, or shipped in from abroad.

pc02.text: Two young men from Sivakasi make that trip. P. Ayya Nadar is about seventeen. A. Shanmuga Nadar is about nineteen.

pc03.text: They aren't going to learn fireworks. They're going to learn one thing: how to make a safety match.

pc04.text: They stay six to eight months, learning from a match-maker named Purna Chandra Roy.

pc05.text: In nineteen twenty-three they come home with German machines and open a match factory. The South-India Lucifer Match Industry.

pc06.text: Piece one: a skill. Matches. Not fireworks yet.

pd01.text: But the heavy German machines are a problem. In a small, remote town, they are costly to run.

pd02.text: So the founders change the plan. They spread the work across the villages around.

pd03.text: And here is the first link back to the dry land. Farming is hard, so many families around need work. Accounts describe plenty of low-cost labour in the villages around Sivakasi, Sattur and Virudhunagar.

pd04.text: Families roll, fill and pack by hand, at home. The factory does only the chemical part.

pd05.text: It fits the mood of the time. Mahatma Gandhi is urging Indians to revive village industries.

pd06.text: Think of many home kitchens feeding one restaurant, instead of one giant kitchen. Cheap to start. Hard to supervise.

pd07.text: Piece two: hands. The weak farms supplied them.

pe01.text: In nineteen twenty-six the two men part ways, and compete. Ayya Nadar's brand is a squirrel, Anil. Shanmuga Nadar's is a crow, Kaaka. A squirrel against a crow.

pe02.text: To stand out, match-makers add something new: sticks that burn in colour. They're called Bengal lights. In Tamil, matthaappu.

pe03.text: Local histories treat the Bengal light as the stepping stone. A match that burns in colour is already close to a sparkler. And in nineteen thirty-eight, N. R. K. Rajarathina Nadar opens the town's first factory made only for fireworks.

pe03b.text: So that is how matches became fireworks. Coloured matches led to fireworks. Not a tradition. A chain.

pe04.text: And now the dryness that hurt the farms starts to help the factories. Paper tubes and chemicals must dry in the open. Dry, sunny Sivakasi dries them for free.

pe05.text: Piece three: the sun. A curse for the farms. A help for the fireworks.

pf01.text: Every matchbox and every packet of crackers needs a bright paper label. In the nineteen thirties, those labels come from presses in Bombay, today's Mumbai.

pf02.text: So in nineteen thirty-eight, K. S. A. Arunagiri Nadar sets up a printing press in Sivakasi itself. National Litho Press.

pf03.text: Picture a shop that sells most of its stock in one week, and keeps running out of paper cups from a far-off city. So the owner buys a printer. Then he notices it can print for the other eleven months too.

pf04.text: That is Sivakasi's second trick. When the fireworks season ends, the presses keep running. Calendars. Diaries. Notebooks.

pf05.text: Prime Minister Nehru is said to have called the town 'Kutty Japan', Little Japan, for making matches, fireworks and print on its own.

pf06.text: A historian of the town, Rengaiah Murugan, put it simply: 'As a chain reaction, various allied industries started to mushroom.'

pg01.text: Now comes the moment that turns a good town into the national one. Nineteen-forty.

pg02.text: That year, the Explosives Rules arrive. To make fireworks, you now need a licence.

pg03.text: Then the Second World War cuts off the fireworks that used to come in from abroad.

pg04.text: The few licensed makers suddenly have the whole market. By nineteen forty-two, three firms hold licences: National, Standard and Kaliswari.

pg05.text: Three licensed factories in nineteen forty-two.

pg06.text: By nineteen eighty: a hundred and eighty-nine.

pg07.text: By two thousand and one: four hundred and fifty.

pg08.text: Today, the industry says, more than a thousand.

pg09.text: Worth about six thousand crore rupees a year. That is sixty billion rupees.

pk01.text: So the paradox dissolves. Weak farms gave Sivakasi hands and sun. A matchbox gave it a skill. A press kept it busy all year. And a war gave it a market.

pk02.text: But the paradox has a second half. The very things that built the town now put it under pressure.

ph00.text: Today's challenge comes from a new direction. The air.

ph01.text: In October twenty-eighteen, the Supreme Court bans crackers made with barium salts, and joined crackers. The aim is cleaner air in the north.

ph02.text: The industry's answer is the green cracker, developed by a government lab, CSIR-NEERI. Its versions are called SWAS, SAFAL and STAR.

ph03.text: Green doesn't mean pollution-free. The lab's own claim is about a third less particle pollution.

ph04.text: How? According to the lab, the mix releases water vapour and air as it burns, which helps the dust settle. Picture a tiny mist sprayer inside the shell.

ph04b.text: Delhi and its surroundings are roughly thirteen percent of national demand, industry associations estimate.

ph05.text: In October twenty twenty-five, the Court eases the Delhi ban: green crackers only, with QR codes, in fixed time slots. But it comes just before Deepavali. A makers' leader said it comes too close to the festival, yet gives hope for future business.

ph06.text: So the law gave a ban, then a lab, then a compromise. And a deadline that arrived too late for this season.

pi01.text: Now go back to the hands. By the industry's count, about three lakh people work in these factories. That is three hundred thousand. Many more work around them.

pi01b.text: Mixing, filling and threading fuses are still done mostly by hand.

pi01c.text: On paper, a small unit's licence limits how many people may work inside. Reports say twelve.

pi02.text: Reports describe sheds sub-let to contractors, and crowded verandahs. A gap between the licence and the workplace.

pi03.text: On the nineteenth of April, twenty twenty-six, an explosion at a factory near Sivakasi killed twenty-five workers.

pi04.text: A worker, K. Rajkumar, told The Hindu that with a biometric attendance system, identifying the dead would not have been so hard.

pi05.text: The choice the founders made in nineteen twenty-three, spread the work across many hands, built the town. Now the same choice needs a new safety answer.

pj00.text: In May twenty twenty-five, the makers' association applied for a GI tag for Sivakasi fireworks. It's a legal label of origin. Their lawyer says it would help curb duplicates.

pj01.text: A matchbox. A coloured flame. A printing press. A war. A hundred years.

pj02.text: So India's fireworks sky wasn't made by an ancient tradition. It was made by a town that kept learning.

pj03.text: A dry town built an industry out of hands and sun. Its next lesson is how to keep those hands safe.
